https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8.text: Image source, Getty Images By Kelly Ng Â and Â Kurumi Mori ,Â Tokyo correspondent Published 3 hours ago Japan has executed a man who killed five people in a gaming parlour fire in 2009, making this the first time in more than a year that the country has enacted the death sentence. Sunao Takami, 58, had doused the pachinko gaming parlour near his home in Osaka with gasoline and set it alight, killing four customers and one employee. A six-member jury and a panel of three judges rejected the defence's argument that Takami was mentally ill at the time of the crime, and sentenced him to hang in 2011. Japan and the United States are the only G7 countries that still impose capital punishment, with death row prisoners in Japan typically being notified of their hanging just a few hours in advance. "We ordered the execution after careful and thorough consideration," Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi said on Friday. This is the first execution carried out under the Takaichi administration. In June last year, Japan executed Takahiro Shiraishi , dubbed the "Twitter killer" , who murdered and dismembered nine people in 2017. Shiraishi's killings came to light in October 2017, when police found body parts in the Japanese city of Zama, near Tokyo, when they were searching for one of the victims. Surveys suggest there is strong public support for the death penalty in Japan. Rights groups, however, have criticised authorities for leaving death-row inmates in solitary confinement for long periods of time, and also pointed to a lack of transparency as to when executions are carried out. The producers said the team had carried out scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes. Photograph: The Guardian NAZA NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems Peter Beaumont Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.45 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war. The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary. In its response, which the IDF said was based on statements made by the film-makers and a review made by a representative who had attended a viewing, the Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on interviews with two dozen intelligence and other troops who had only a partial picture of the target approval process. NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiere Read more At the centre of the IDF’s rebuttal was its often repeated claim that its rules of engagement explicitly distinguish between militants and civilians and prohibit deliberately targeting civilians, while requiring commanders to take steps to minimise civilian harm, claims that have long been challenged over the years by critics. While acknowledging that it used AI to help recommend potential targets in Gaza , the IDF also said final decisions made on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers. The IDF also denied that it had approved, planned or carried out an attack anticipating 500 civilian casualties in pursuit of a single Hamas target. The IDF statement follows previous efforts by Israeli politicians to dismiss NAZA – a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike – which have accompanied death threats against the film’s directors , Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and calls by the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for them to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship . It also echoed previous complaints by some Israeli critics – including journalists – that the film’s military sources were anonymised, despite the fact that source protection in media investigations is commonplace and regarded by much of the media as an ethical requirement. “The film NAZA presents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal,” the statement added. Responding to the IDF statement, the Guardian, which produced the film, disclosed further details of how the team had verified the allegations which involved scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes. A spokesperson said: “The IDF’s attempt to portray the 24 participants in NAZA as junior-ranking officers involved only in the early stages of the targeting process is false. “They include officers and soldiers who were involved in multiple stages of the targeting process in Gaza, including intelligence, operations and the final authorisation process. View image in fullscreen People walk past the rubble of destroyed buildings in Jabaliya in the northern Gaza Strip. Photograph: Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters “The process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film. “Over the past three years we have together interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes. “The Guardian stands fully behind the film, which builds on three years of detailed reporting by the Guardian and our partners. Several highly respected news organisations have subsequently confirmed the IDF’s use of AI-driven systems in the Gaza offensive and the loosening of safeguards to protect civilians, including the New York Times, Washington Post and Associated Press.” While Netanyahu has claimed that Israeli military safeguards have led to one of the lowest civilian-combatant ratios in modern warfare, that has been challenged by the IDF’s own leaked casualty assessments, by the UN’s commission of inquiry in 2024 and research by NGOs including Action on Armed Violence. -- 1:55 NAZA - official trailer Explore more on these topics NAZA Gaza Palestine Israel Documentary films Israel-Gaza war Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Gaza documentary NAZA beats Avengers Endgame: Encore to top Italian box office NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiere Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film Netanyahu seeks to strip citizenship from Israelis as threats to NAZA film directors intensify ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZA Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/couples-looking-to.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O7ON After Russia's invasion of Ukraine, much of the surrogacy industry shifted to Georgia Image: SWR Advertisement Three years ago, Olga, 40, and Daniel (both names changed to protect the their identities) from Hamburg decided to employ the services of a surrogate mother. But surrogacy is illegal in Germany, and people whose children are born through surrogacy must pursue the legal recognition of their parenthood in German courts. Olga is a German citizen, but was born and raised in Russia . That's why the couple wanted to learn more about the surrogacy market in Russia. But foreign customers have been banned from signing Russian surrogacy contracts since 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , many international agencies that liaise between surrogates and intended parents moved to Georgia . So, Olga and Daniel traveled there. Georgia the new destination for surrogate mothers In the past years, Georgia, a mountainous country in the Caucasus region, has become a sort of surrogacy hub, with women traveling from all over the world to work as surrogates. According to Georgia's Public Service Development Agency, over 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in 2023 across the country. Since 2012, they've given birth to over 5,000 children. And since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, the number of children born to surrogate mothers has skyrocketed. While an estimated 300 surrogate mothers gave birth in 2021, that number leapt to over 1,100 by 2023. Anastasia, 39, is a surrogate mother from Russia working in Georgia. She has a grown daughter and has already seen through three surrogate pregnancies. Her first was in 2021, which she used to finance a property down payment. Surrogacy in the US: a different path to parenthood To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Anastasia says she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted, and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant. "I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She says she's ready to become a surrogate mother again. Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in Tbilisi or Batumi are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge. Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example. Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers." Both work in the medical field, and Olga says perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she says. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga adds. In the spring of 2024, the married couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment. "They had initially told us that the surrogate would spent the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel tell DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war." Human rights experts criticize legislation Georgian laws have a weak spot, the human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze tells DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents, and the clinics, but they do not consider the roles that agencies play. In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the involved parties. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms. Surrogacy laws and rules vary widely across Africa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program, or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination. Agencies guided by material interests "Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya from the University of Leeds tell DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents." Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," Olga says. And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga recounts. "I felt like I was being manipulated." The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now. Mark Sheider and Asja Lokina contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Russian. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/10/17/elon.text: Menü Kereső Telegraph: Musk javasolta Trumpnak a Starlink lassítását Ukrajnában Külföld Ignácz Péter Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Elon Musk javasolta Donald Trump amerikai elnöknek, hogy lassítsák le a Starlink katonai verziójának, a Starshieldnek működését Ukrajnába, amit az ukránok az orosz drónok elleni védekezésre, és támadásokra is használnak – írta a Telegraph brit lap, négy forrásra hivatkozva. A lap egyik forrása szerint Trump egyetértett az ötlettel, ami lehetővé tette a rendszer lassítását. Emiatt az ukránok nem tudtak védekezni a nagy sebességgel haladó sugárhajtású orosz drónok ellen. A rendszer korlátozásáról a hét közepén számolt be Szerhij Beskrestnov, Volodimir Zelenszkij katonai tanácsadója. Elon Musk szerdán azt írta a közösségi oldalán , hogy a Starshield rendszert az amerikai kormány működteti, és annak korlátozásáról az amerikai hadsereg és végső soron az amerikai elnök dönt. Kemény üzenet volt , ahogy egyik napról a másikra visszavágták az ukrán hadsereg hozzáférését Musk műholdas rendszeréhez. Arról, hogy a Starshield miért fontos, és milyen hatásai voltak lassításának, ebből a cikkünkből tudhat meg többet. A rendszer kedd esti lelassítása után Oroszország 39 ballisztikus rakétával 120 drónnal támadta Kijev és Harkiv régióját. A támadások több erőművet és a fővárosba áramot szállító kulcsfontosságú alállomásokat érintettek, köztük egy nagy teljesítményű erőművet is, emiatt Zelenszkij szerint 600 ezer ember maradt áram nélkül. A Telegraph egyik magas rangú forrása szerint Musk azután hárította el magától a felelősséget, hogy megrémült attól, hogy a kedd esti támadások ártani fognak a cége hírnevének Európában. „Azt írta, hogy ártatlan, és hogy az amerikai kormányzat követte el a dolgot. A valóság azonban az, hogy mindketten benne voltak” – mondta a lap forrása. Ezt a Telegraph cikke szerint egy magas rangú európai tisztviselő, valamint két jól értesült ukrán forrás is megerősítettek az események ezen változatát. A Reuters csütörtökön arról számolt be két amerikai és egy európai tisztviselőre hivatkozva, hogy a rendszer lassítására a Fehér Házból kapott utasítást az amerikai védelmi minisztérium. Azt nem közölték, hogy az utasítást ki adta ki. A Politicónak egy névtelenséget kérő amerikai kormányzati tisztviselő azt mondta, hogy a parancs nem az elnöktől érkezett. Pénteken Donald Trump riporterek kérdésére válaszolva tagadta , hogy neki, vagy Musknak köze lett volna a Starshield korlátozásához. Fontos szereplő Musk űrvállalata, a SpaceX az ukrajnai háború egyik legbefolyásosabb, egyben legvitatottabb magánszektorból érkező szereplője. Miután Ukrajnában 2022 februárjában az orosz invázió után akadozni kezdett a net, az azóta már leváltott Mihajlo Fedorov ukrán miniszterelnök-helyettes úgy döntött, segítséget kér a milliárdostól. Musk fél napon belül válaszolt, és a SpaceX műholdas szolgáltatását, a Starlinket küldte az ukránok segítségére . Ezért, mint később kiderült, 3 millió dollárt kapott az Egyesült Államoktól. A műholdas rendszer azóta mélyen beépült az ukrán katonai műveletekbe, a hadsereg tagjai ezen keresztül kommunikálnak és hangolják össze a hadműveleteket. A technológiát az ukrán drónos bevetéseknél is használják, hogy nagyobb távolságokon is tudja tartani a kezelő a kapcsolatot a drónnal. Musk az ukránoknak is csak a saját területükön engedélyezi a Starlink használatát, azaz az oroszok által megszállt ukrán területeken működik a műholdas szolgáltatás, Oroszországban viszont korlátozva van. Korábban is előfordult azonban, hogy Musk önkényesen beavatkozott abba, hogy mikor és hol legyen használhatatlan a Starlink. 2023-ban például elismerte, hogy egy évvel korábban titokban utasította a mérnökeit, hogy kapcsolják le a Starlink műholdas kommunikációs hálózatát a krími partok közelében, hogy megzavarjanak egy ukrán támadást az orosz haditengerészeti flotta ellen. Musk akkor azzal érvelt a döntése mellett, hogy „ mini Pearl Harbort” akadályozott meg vele. 2023-ban aztán megint korlátozták az ukrán hadsereg Starlink-elérését, mert a SpaceX szerint nem kommunikációra, hanem drónok irányítására használták azt. Végül a Pentagon kötött szerződést a SpaceX-szel , és megvásárolták a Starlink szolgáltatását Ukrajnának. Kapcsolódó Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Matt Goodwin wanted Times Radio listeners to believe that Nigel Farage was actually a buffer against racism in Reform. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Matt Goodwin wanted Times Radio listeners to believe that Nigel Farage was actually a buffer against racism in Reform. Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian The politics sketch Reform UK ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples John Crace While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.42 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.44 EDT Share I t was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic. Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear. The only MP to take to X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags. Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires. The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged a bullet. Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox. To put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants. It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion After the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is | Owen Jones Read more Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed. Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war. All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war. Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?
